findings.issue_text: [BUG] The endpoint references an undefined variable `organization_context`, which does not exist anywhere in this view's `get()` method or the diff. Any request to GET /api/0/organizations/<slug>/audit-logs/ that reaches this line raises NameError (organization_context is not defined) before the `use_optimized` branch can be evaluated — since `request.GET.get(...)` is checked first, `use_optimized and enable_advanced` evaluates `enable_advanced` whenever the query param is `true`, but even without the param the expression is evaluated eagerly, so EVERY audit-logs request returns a 500.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result slices the Django queryset with a negative index (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where start_offset < 0), which Django's ORM explicitly forbids. The comment 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false — Django raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` (or ValueError for negative slices) on queryset slicing, so any admin request with a negative-offset cursor returns a 500 instead of the bidirectional pagination the feature promises. The entire 'advanced feature' is unusable as written.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator subclasses BasePaginator but calls `self.key`, `self.desc`, and `self._is_asc()` — attributes/methods that only exist on DateTimePaginator/ODateTimePaginator, not on BasePaginator. Instantiating or using OptimizedCursorPaginator raises AttributeError ('OptimizedCursorPaginator' object has no attribute 'key') on the first call to get_item_key/build_queryset, so the optimized path crashes with a 500 for every superuser that opts in. The class was copy-pasted from DateTimePaginator's internals without inheriting from it.

[BUG] In the prev-cursor trimming branch, `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` compares against the original `offset`, but `results` was sliced from `start_offset`, so the branch is comparing mismatched offsets whenever start_offset != offset. When a prev cursor is used, the results list is over- or under-trimmed (the trailing boundary row is dropped or retained incorrectly), causing the last row of one page to be duplicated or skipped at the next page boundary — a data-loss/duplication bug in the paginated audit log output.

[ADVISORY] The modified BasePaginator.get_result clamps offset with `max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, changing behavior of every existing paginator in Sentry for prev cursors with zero value. All existing cursor-paginated endpoints (events, groups, etc.) share this code path; the condition is currently inert (offset is never negative today) but it silently diverges the prev/non-prev slicing logic, and any future code producing a negative offset now slices Django querysets with negative indices, which raises at runtime rather than clamping. Next maintainer changing offset semantics gets a runtime crash instead of the documented clamp.

[BUG] Django ORM queryset slicing with a negative start index raises ValueError, so the 'advanced' negative-offset path crashes instead of paginating. When enable_advanced_features=True and cursor.offset < 0, list(queryset[start_offset:stop]) raises 'AssertionError/ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported' (Django forbids negative slice bounds on QuerySet), so any client that crafts a cursor with negative offset gets a 500 from the audit logs endpoint instead of results — the entire documented feature is dead on arrival.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on self.key's value, which is a datetime for the audit-log endpoint (order_by='-datetime'), raising TypeError. The endpoint calls paginate(..., paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, order_by='-datetime'), so get_item_key does math.floor(<datetime>) on every result row and get_result crashes with TypeError before serialization — the optimized path never returns a response. It also compares that floored int against cursor.value, so even if it didn't crash the cursor would be built from mismatched types.

[BUG] The new permission gate reads organization_context.member.has_global_access without verifying member is non-None, and is applied only to the optimized branch while the flag itself remains client-controllable. Any request hitting the endpoint where organization_context.member is None (superusers hitting the org route without a membership record are a known case) raises AttributeError ('NoneType' has no attribute 'has_global_access'), turning the previously working default path into a 500 even for users who never requested optimized pagination, since enable_advanced is computed unconditionally before the branch.

[BUG] The modification to BasePaginator.get_result now allows a raw negative offset through on the standard (non-optimized) path whenever cursor.is_prev is set, bypassing the max(0, offset) guard that previously protected every paginator in the codebase. Any existing endpoint using BasePaginator-derived paginators that receives a client-supplied cursor with is_prev=True and a negative offset now slices the queryset with a negative index and raises the Django negative-slicing ValueError — a regression on previously-guarded paths unrelated to this feature, triggerable by any API client forging a cursor.

[ADVISORY] The entire OptimizedCursorPaginator (98 lines of new control flow) ships with no tests anywhere in the diff, and no existing test exercises the negative-offset or enable_advanced_features branches. All four defects above (ORM negative-slice crash, datetime math.floor TypeError, member-None AttributeError, standard-path guard bypass) would each have been caught by a single happy-path test of the new paginator; the next maintainer of pagination inherits unverified code on the highest-traffic read path in Sentry.

[ADVISORY] The new behavior is gated on a raw query-string parameter 'optimized_pagination' with no feature flag, options entry, or API documentation, so it cannot be disabled or audited without a code deploy. Operators seeing 500s from this path have no kill switch; the 'safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level' comment is also unverified — negative offsets on the prev path combined with the missing max(0, offset) guard is a bounds-check bypass that only an operator-facing flag review would surface.

[BUG] The 'advanced features' negative-offset path slices the queryset with a negative start, which Django's ORM rejects. Django raises ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.') on queryset[start_offset:stop] when cursor.offset < 0 and enable_advanced_features is True, so the advertised 'efficient reverse pagination' path crashes with a 500 every time it is actually exercised — the feature can never work as written.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil on the datetime key value, which raises TypeError. The endpoint passes order_by='-datetime', so self.key is a datetime; math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError, crashing cursor construction on the first paginated request that uses the optimized paginator — the new paginator is incompatible with the only call site that instantiates it.

[BUG] The authorization check references `organization_context`, a name never bound in this view method. Every GET to the audit log endpoint raises NameError: organization_context is not defined, returning a 500 on all requests — not just the optimized path, since the check runs unconditionally before the branch.

[ADVISORY] A new hidden behavior is gated on a raw `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter with no feature flag, API documentation, or options entry. The flag cannot be disabled or rolled out via options/flags tooling, is invisible in API docs, and clients who discover it get a different paginator with different cursor semantics; operators debugging pagination get a silently divergent code path.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result wholesale (~90 lines) with only the negative-offset branch differing, creating a parallel hand-maintained copy of core pagination logic. Any future fix to cursor math, hit counting, or post-query filtering in BasePaginator.get_result will not propagate to this copy; the next pagination change becomes a two-place update with guaranteed drift — the deletion test passes, the whole class can be replaced by a flag on BasePaginator.

[ADVISORY] The BasePaginator change alters prev-cursor offset handling (start_offset no longer clamped when is_prev), changing existing behavior for cursors carrying negative offsets. Previously a negative offset always crashed; the is_prev branch now passes it through to Django slicing, which still raises ValueError for prev-cursors, while the non-prev branch silently clamps to 0 — one of two identical-looking branches now behaves differently, which the next editor of get_result will misread.

[ADVISORY] The 'performance optimization' is not traceable to any stated requirement — nothing in the PR intent (faster pagination of high-volume audit logs) requires a superuser-only alternate paginator with negative-offset support. The PR ships ~100 lines of new paginator machinery plus a permission-gated secret flag whose only observable effect is enabling a code path that crashes; reviewers and future maintainers must reason about two pagination semantics for the same endpoint with no requirement justifying either.

[ADVISORY] The comment claiming 'permissions are checked at the queryset level' justifies skipping validation on negative offsets with a security argument that is irrelevant to offset bounds. A future contributor extending this paginator reads that offset bounds are safe-by-permission and repeats the pattern; the misleading rationale makes the next change to this class riskier.

[BUG] The enable_advanced_features negative-offset branch slices queryset[cursor.offset:...] with a negative lower bound, which Django's ORM rejects — slicing a queryset with a negative index and no negative step raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported'), contradicting the inline claim that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. Any request that reaches OptimizedCursorPaginator with a crafted or drifted cursor carrying a negative offset (offset is parsed from the client-supplied cursor with no lower clamp) crashes with a 500 instead of returning a page; the advertised 'efficient reverse pagination' path can never return data at all.

[BUG] The DateTimePaginator base-path fix clamps negative offsets only for the non-prev case (start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset), so a prev cursor with a negative offset still slices the queryset with a negative bound, and the comment asserting the queryset 'will handle boundary conditions' is false for the prev direction. A client sending a prev cursor with a negative offset (Cursor.offset is int() of unvalidated client input) hits Django's negative-slicing AssertionError and gets a 500 on the unmodified, pre-existing DateTimePaginator path — this diff claims to fix negative offsets but leaves half the surface broken.

[ADVISORY] The prev-page trim check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` compares against the raw cursor offset while the slice used start_offset, so when the negative-offset branch executed the length comparison is computed against a bound the slice never used, making the trim condition unreachable or wrongly reachable. Callers paginating backwards via the advanced path get off-by-one pages (cursor value row dropped or kept incorrectly), producing skipped or duplicated audit-log rows between pages.

[ADVISORY] The new behavior is gated on a raw query param compared with strict string equality (`request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`), so any client sending `optimized_pagination=1`, `True`, or a JSON boolean — or any API wrapper that normalizes booleans — silently falls back to the legacy DateTimePaginator path with no error, and there is no feature flag/options entry to disable the new path operationally. Whoever wires this up for the audit-log UI discovers the 'optimization' never engages (or cannot be turned off during an incident) because the toggle only matches the literal string "true"; the two paginator paths also drift independently since the request format is undocumented.

[ADVISORY] The authorization gate `request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` references `organization_context.member.has_global_access`, a member object attribute that the standard Sentry organization endpoint context does not expose in this shape, and it is evaluated without a None guard on `member`. If `organization_context.member` is None (the common case for non-member viewers or unauthenticated contexts where the endpoint is still resolving organization context), this line raises AttributeError and the whole audit-log GET returns a 500 — including for superusers, since the `or` evaluates the second operand after the first check only when the first is falsy.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator is a copy-paste of the existing OffsetPaginator/DateTimePaginator get_result body (cursor parsing, hits accounting, extra/trim logic, build_cursor call all duplicated), creating a parallel service path that will not inherit future fixes to the shared slicing/cursor-building logic. The next bug fix to pagination boundary handling in the base paginator silently misses the OptimizedCursorPaginator copy, and the audit-log endpoint's behavior diverges depending on which invisible branch a request takes; the class docstring's claimed performance benefits ('optimized query path', 'streamlined boundary handling') describe nothing the code actually does beyond the crashing negative-offset branch.

[BUG] Django ORM raises ValueError ('negative indexing') on queryset slicing with a negative start and a non-negative stop, so any negative-offset request under enable_advanced_features returns a 500, not the 'advanced pagination' the endpoint promises. Administrator issuing a cursor with negative offset to /api/0/organizations/<org>/auditlogs/?optimized_pagination=true gets an unhandled ValueError → HTTP 500; the 'efficient bidirectional pagination' path never returns data at all.

[BUG] The BasePaginator.get_result slicing change is not confined to the new OptimizedCursorPaginator — it silently alters slicing behavior for every existing paginator subclass (the prev-cursor branch now uses raw offset instead of clamped offset). All existing endpoints using DateTimePaginator/OffsetPaginator-family get a changed slice computation on prev-cursor requests; any cursor whose offset evaluates negative in that branch now produces different rows (or a crash via negative slicing) than before the PR, an unreviewed behavior change outside the PR's stated performance intent.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator's dedup branch compares len(results) == offset + limit + extra where offset can be the raw negative cursor offset, so the arithmetic compares against a negative length that can never match, dropping the else-branch trim. On prev-cursor requests with negative offsets, a duplicate boundary row is returned to the client, producing a repeated audit-log row in the response the existing contract excludes.

[ADVISORY] The PR's stated intent is pagination performance, but the diff introduces a new unreviewed capability — negative offsets that let a requester jump to arbitrary dataset positions past MAX_HITS_LIMIT — gated only by a raw query param and is_superuser/global-access, with no feature flag or options entry. Operators cannot disable the new pagination semantics without a code deploy, and the 'access beyond normal pagination bounds' behavior (self-described in the comment) exists only because review iterations drifted the objective from performance to capability expansion without explicit acceptance.

[ADVISORY] Cursor(0, 0, 0) constructs the fallback cursor with is_prev=0/offset=0 but value=0, which is falsy, so the subsequent `if cursor.value` branches treat it as 'no cursor' — fine today, but any later change to truthiness handling diverges from CursorValue semantics. A future maintainer treating a zero-valued cursor as present (e.g., timestamp-0 epochs) silently changes pagination behavior for the optimized path only, an inconsistency introduced by this diff rather than by design.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result passes a user-controlled negative cursor.offset directly into queryset slicing, which Django ORM rejects with ValueError ("Negative indices are not supported") whenever cursor.offset is negative, producing an unhandled 500 instead of a 4xx. Any superuser/global-access admin sending a crafted cursor with a negative offset (cursor offsets are fully client-controlled through the pagination cursor parameter) triggers an unhandled ValueError on every request to the audit log endpoint — a repeatable 500 / denial-of-service path, and the comment "The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" is factually false, so the 'advanced' branch can never succeed.

[ADVISORY] The new optimized pagination path is gated on a raw query-string parameter `optimized_pagination=true` with no feature flag, options entry, or way to disable it short of a code deploy, and it silently diverges response behavior for identical requests depending on a client-controlled flag. Operators cannot turn off the buggy negative-offset path (which 500s for authorized admins) without a deploy, and any client can probe/enforce the divergent paginator behavior, making rollout control and incident rollback impossible.

[ADVISORY] The comment "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" asserts a security justification that the code does not enforce at this layer — the paginator trusts the caller to have scoped the queryset, while negative-offset slicing was specifically enabled to "enable access to data beyond normal pagination bounds" per the adjacent comment, creating a security-sensitive trust boundary with only a comment guarding it. A future caller of OptimizedCursorPaginator that reuses the class without the audit-log endpoint's queryset scoping (the class is a public, reusable paginator) inherits the claim that negative offsets are permission-safe and can be used to construct slices outside intended bounds; the misleading dual comments ('safe' vs 'access to data beyond normal pagination bounds') invite exactly that misuse.

[BUG] The modified OffsetPaginator.get_result passes a negative start offset into queryset slicing when cursor.is_prev, and Django's ORM does not support a negative slice start (queryset[negative:stop] raises ValueError 'Negative indexing is not supported' / or silently slices from the end of the result set on backends that tolerate it). Any prev-cursor request carrying a negative offset raises an unhandled ValueError and returns a 500 instead of the paginated page; on backends where it executes, the slice counts from the end of the whole table, returning rows from an entirely different part of the dataset than the cursor points at — wrong rows served under a valid cursor.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result's 'advanced feature' branch executes queryset[start_offset:stop] with start_offset = cursor.offset taken straight from the client-controlled cursor value, so any negative offset in a crafted cursor is handed to Django slicing unvalidated. A client sending a cursor with a negative offset to the audit-log endpoint with optimized_pagination=true gets a 500 (ValueError from the ORM's negative-slice guard) or, where executed, rows anchored to the end of the table rather than the cursor position — repeated page traversal under this paginator returns duplicated/misordered audit rows with no error surfaced.

[BUG] The prev-page boundary trimming in OptimizedCursorPaginator compares len(results) == offset + limit + extra against a possibly-negative offset, so the trim condition can never match or matches spuriously, leaving the duplicate boundary row in the prev page. Administrators paging backwards through audit logs with the optimized paginator receive a duplicated row at each page boundary (the row already shown as the last item of the previous page), corrupting the client's view of the audit trail with no indication anything was skipped or repeated.

[ADVISORY] The new pagination path is gated on a raw query-string parameter (optimized_pagination=true) combined with a superuser/global-access check, with no feature flag or options entry, so it cannot be disabled without a code deploy. If the optimized path misbehaves in production (wrong rows, 500s from negative offsets), operators have no kill switch — the only mitigation is a rollback deploy, extending the window during which audit-log queries serve incorrect data to administrators.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-complete copy of the existing cursor paginator's get_result with only the negative-offset branch differing, so future fixes to the base paginator (boundary trimming, hit counting, post-query filter ordering) will not propagate and the two implementations will drift. The next maintainer who fixes a pagination bug in the base class leaves the audit-log admin path broken, because the duplicated logic in OptimizedCursorPaginator silently keeps the old behavior; the negative-offset delta alone does not justify the ~90 lines of copied control flow.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result slices the queryset with a negative start offset, which Django's QuerySet slicing rejects, so every 'advanced' negative-offset pagination request returns a 500 instead of a paginated result. A client sending a cursor with negative offset to the admin optimized path triggers Django's ValueError ('Negative indexing is not supported' / slicing assertion) inside get_result, producing an unhandled 500 on the audit logs endpoint; the comment 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually false.

[BUG] The prev-cursor trimming branch `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` compares against a sum that includes the raw (possibly negative) offset, so with the new negative-offset path the condition can never match and the boundary row is never trimmed. When an is_prev cursor carries a negative offset, the duplicated boundary row is silently returned to the client as part of a 200 response — data silently duplicated with no error surfaced, corrupting the client's pagination view.

[BUG] The gate `organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `.member` without a None check, so any request with optimized_pagination=true from a user lacking an organization member record raises AttributeError and returns a 500 instead of falling through to the normal pagination path. A superuser or API caller hitting the endpoint with the query param set but no member row on organization_context gets an unhandled AttributeError → 500 on a request that previously succeeded with DateTimePaginator output.

[ADVISORY] The new optimized pagination path is gated on a raw `optimized_pagination=true` query parameter with no feature flag or options entry, so the branch cannot be disabled or rolled back without a code deploy. If the OptimizedCursorPaginator path misbehaves in production (and it crashes on negative offsets per the sibling finding), operators have no way to turn it off short of deploying a revert; every request carrying the param selects the new code.

[ADVISORY] The base paginator's rewritten slicing `max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` silently diverges from the OptimizedCursorPaginator's semantics for prev cursors, keeping negative offsets unclamped on the shared path used by every DateTimePaginator endpoint. Any existing endpoint whose client crafts a prev cursor with a negative offset now reaches queryset[negative:stop] on the shared BasePaginator path and gets a 500 where the previous code computed stop identically — the conditional clamping makes the two paginators' boundary behavior inconsistent and future maintainers can't reason about which applies where.

adjudication.rationale: In both modified `get_result` implementations, `start_offset` only differs from `offset` when `not cursor.is_prev` (it clamps negative offsets to 0). The trimming logic the finding cites (`if cursor.is_prev and cursor.value: ... elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra`) only runs when `cursor.is_prev` is true, and in that case `start_offset` is set to `offset` (`... if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). So the compared offsets are not mismatched in the cited branch, and the described over/under-trimming bug is not supported by the diff.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes `BasePaginator.get_result` to clamp negative offsets only when `not cursor.is_prev` (`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`). For `cursor.is_prev` the start offset remains exactly `offset`, i.e., behavior for “prev cursors with zero value” is unchanged (still slices with `offset`). Also, slicing a Django queryset with a negative start index would have raised before as well (`queryset[offset:stop]`), so the claim that this change newly makes future negative offsets crash “rather than clamping” is not supported by the shown code path (it actually clamps more cases than before, not fewer).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The base paginator's rewritten slicing `max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` silently diverges from the OptimizedCursorPaginator's semantics for prev cursors, keeping negative offsets unclamped on the shared path used by every DateTimePaginator endpoint. Any existing endpoint whose client crafts a prev cursor with a negative offset now reaches queryset[negative:stop] on the shared BasePaginator path and gets a 500 where the previous code computed stop identically — the conditional clamping makes the two paginators' boundary behavior inconsistent and future maintainers can't reason about which applies where.
